outline.description: Sets the stage for the dispute by describing who the parties are, why the records were sought, how the FBI processed the request, and how the case moved through the district court to the D.C. Circuit.
subtopics: Foad Farahi’s immigration history and DHS removal proceedings; FBI agent’s testimony about alleged terrorist connections
FOIA request to the FBI for Farahi’s file; scope of potentially responsive material (about 10,750 pages and 80 CDs)
Agency processing over several years; partial releases and extensive withholdings
FBI’s October 2019 summary-judgment motion supported by a public declaration from David Hardy (RIDS Section Chief) and an ex parte, sealed supplemental declaration

District court’s November 2022 order: finding the government had ‘seemingly’ met Exemption 7(A) but requiring updated proof due to staleness and more information on segregability; denial without prejudice
FBI’s renewed motion with public and ex parte declarations from Joseph Bender (then Acting RIDS Section Chief), confirming investigations remained ongoing and addressing segregability
District court’s grant of summary judgment on the renewed motion; crediting the ongoing-proceedings showing and the segregability explanation; Farahi’s appeal to the D.C. Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Governing FOIA Framework and Standards of Review
outline.description: Explains the statutory and doctrinal rules the court applied, including Exemption 7(A), the burden of proof, the standard of review, deference principles in national-security contexts, the segregability requirement, and the handling of category-based withholdings and ex parte submissions.
subtopics: FOIA’s basic rule of disclosure and exemptions: 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(3), (b)

Exemption 7(A): records compiled for law-enforcement purposes whose disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings; proceedings must be pending or reasonably anticipated (CREW; Mapother)
Standard of review: de novo review of summary judgment; government’s burden under § 552(a)(4)(B)
Deference to the FBI as a law-enforcement agency (Campbell; Clemente) and heightened deference where national security is implicated (CNSS)
Proving Exemption 7(A) via agency declarations; reliance on reasonably specific affidavits, including ex parte submissions where necessary (CREW; Perioperative Services)
Ongoing criminal investigations as qualifying ‘proceedings’; attestation to their existence can suffice (CREW; Juarez)

Segregability duty: release any reasonably segregable, non-exempt information; denial permitted when non-exempt matter is inextricably intertwined with exempt material (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii), (b); Mead; Juarez)
Category-by-category withholdings must be sufficiently distinct (Gallant; CREW); forfeiture doctrine on inadequately developed arguments (Khine)
Clarifying note: although the opinion at one point cites § 552(b)(7)(B) when discussing ‘interference with enforcement proceedings,’ the analysis applies Exemption 7(A)

outline.description: Analyzes how the court determined that the withheld records were compiled for law-enforcement purposes under Exemption 7(A).
subtopics: Rational nexus requirement: link between the investigation and the FBI’s law-enforcement duties, and between the subject and a possible security risk or violation of federal law (Pratt; Campbell)

Hardy’s public declaration: records compiled in furtherance of investigations of national security and international terrorism violations, including pending law-enforcement proceedings and Farahi’s associations
Supplemental details provided in Hardy’s ex parte declaration
Context corroborating the nexus: Farahi’s concessions below and public allegations from immigration proceedings regarding ties to designated terrorist organizations and individuals
Holding on this prong: the FBI carried its burden; the nexus is clear and entitled to deference

outline.chapter_title: Interference with Pending or Reasonably Anticipated Proceedings
outline.description: Explains the court’s reasoning that disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with ongoing or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceedings, addressing the passage-of-time challenge and the role of the Hardy and Bender declarations.
subtopics: Recognized harms: disclosure could tip off targets to the scope and direction of an ongoing investigation (CNSS support for this rationale)
Proof of pendency: CREW allows the government to establish ongoing proceedings by attesting to their existence; Juarez underscores applicability while evidence is being gathered
Hardy’s public and ex parte declarations establishing an ongoing investigation and interference risk; Bender’s later declaration confirming ongoing status as of March 2023
Addressing staleness: district court’s interim order sought an update; Bender’s terse confirmation viewed in context as an update rather than standalone proof
Court’s evaluation of Farahi’s conclusoriness argument: combined declarations and prior ‘seemingly’ sufficient showing satisfied CREW’s specificity concerns
Plausibility reinforced by breadth and nature of the investigation as publicly alleged in immigration proceedings
Holding on this prong: the FBI met its burden to show a concrete, ongoing or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceeding would be jeopardized by disclosure

outline.chapter_title: Segregability, Ex Parte Reliance, and Remaining Arguments
outline.description: Covers the segregability analysis, the propriety of ex parte declarations, the forfeited category-based challenge, and the ultimate disposition and implications.
subtopics: Segregability standard: agencies must release reasonably segregable, non-exempt material; denial is proper when non-exempt information is inextricably intertwined or only random, non-meaningful snippets remain (5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(8)(A)(ii), (b); Mead; Juarez; Perioperative Services)
District court’s reliance on Bender’s supplemental ex parte submission to find no reasonably segregable material and its ‘detailed justification’
‘Information, not words’ principle: why scattered words or phrases interspersed line-by-line do not amount to meaningful, segregable information (Mead)

Use of ex parte declarations: permissible and sometimes necessary to avoid revealing the very material at issue; Farahi did not object below and cannot challenge reliance on appeal (Perioperative Services)
Category-by-category withholding challenge: requirement that categories be sufficiently distinct (Gallant; CREW), but Farahi forfeited the argument by not developing it (Khine)

Disposition: Affirmance of summary judgment for the FBI; practical takeaways for FOIA litigants and agencies, including the value of updated declarations to address staleness and the deference accorded in national-security investigations
